sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Okay, learn astro once and you can read the big words in every space book, from astronaut to astronomical."
READ each word as it appears, then connect astro to the card meaning: star.
astronaut - astro means star + naut means sailor: a sailor among the stars. A person who travels into space.
astronomy - astro means star + nomy means law or order: the laws of the stars. The science of stars and planets.
astronomer - astro means star + nom means law + -er means a person who: a person who studies the laws of the stars.
astronomical - astro means star + nom means law + -ical means relating to: relating to the stars. It also means huge, as huge as the distances in space.
astrology - astro means star + -logy means talk: star talk. The belief that stars shape your life. It is not science.
astrophysics - astro means star + physics means the science of energy and forces: the physics of the stars.
asteroid - aster is astro's twin spelling, meaning star + -oid means like: like a star. A space rock that looked like a star in old telescopes.
asterisk - aster means star + -isk means little: a little star. The * symbol.
astrolabe - astro means star + labe means taker: a star-taker. An old tool sailors used to measure how high the stars were.
Memory hook: point up at the night sky when you say astro, then swap astro for 'star' and read the rest: astronaut, star sailor. Challenge: catch an astro word in a space book or the news by Tuesday.
sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "Okay, when you finish, write one sentence that shows the difference between an astronaut and an astronomer."
2. CHECK: the sentence must show that one travels into space and one studies the stars from Earth.
EXTENSION: Write the full morpheme sum for astronomical, then one sentence where it means about the stars and one where it means huge.
Answer: e.g. astronomical = astro (star) + nom (law) + -ical (relating to). The astronomical society meets on Fridays. / The ticket prices were astronomical.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Swap vague verbs like gets, goes, makes and says for verbs that show exactly what happens, with a strength that fits the facts.
WHY THIS WEEK: last week's nouns told the reader exactly who or what. Vague verbs still make an argument sound flat, because the reader cannot see what is happening.
TIME: 5 minutes, no more - I do 1 min, We do 1 question, You do 3 questions at about 45 seconds each. One question per slide; your click reveals the answer.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards - books, fingers and voices only.
PREP: a verb is the doing or saying word. Three upgrades this week: exact (exactly what happens?), strength (does it fit the facts? too strong is hyperbole), saying verbs (how was it said?).

i_do.title: Swap the vague verb
i_do.rule: Upgrade a vague verb to one that shows exactly what happens.
i_do.example:
Litter gets into our creek.
Litter washes into our creek.
items: Vague verbs: gets, goes, makes, does, has.
i_do.footer: Tomorrow: a verb with the right strength
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: gets becomes washes - it shows exactly how the litter moves.
1. SAY: "Okay, last week we upgraded nouns. Today, verbs. A vague verb like gets hides what really happens, so your reader cannot see the problem."
2. WRITE: copy "Litter gets into our creek." on the class board. POINT at gets and ask aloud, exactly what happens?
3. WRITE: cross out gets and write washes above it, so the board reads "Litter washes into our creek."
4. ASK: "Which sentence lets you see the problem? One finger for the first, two for the second, voices off, show me." 5 sec. EXPECT: two fingers - washes.
TRAP: keeping the vague verb and adding to it, like really gets. Fix: say the verb itself must change, student swaps gets for washes.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether gets is wrong, say it is not wrong, just vague - washes shows how the litter moves, so the reader sees it.
---
Purpose: day one shows the exact-verb upgrade on one argument sentence. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: vague verbs (get, go, make, do, have) fit almost any sentence, so they show nothing; an exact verb (washes, digs, melts) shows the action.

we_do.title: Which verb shows it?
we_do.rule: Pick the sentence that shows exactly what happens.

round.prompt:
A) Plastic bags do harm to turtles.
B) Plastic bags choke turtles.
round.why: choke shows what happens; do harm is vague
round.notes:
ANSWER: B - choke shows exactly what the bags do.
1. SAY: "Okay, two arguments about turtles. Read both in your head."
2. ASK: "Which one shows exactly what happens? One finger for A, two for B, voices off, show me on three." 5 sec. EXPECT: two fingers - B.
3. REVEAL after fingers are scanned. ASK: "How do you know?" Cold call one student. EXPECT: choke shows what happens; do harm could mean anything.
4. WRITE: copy A on the class board, cross out do harm to and write choke above it, so the board now matches B.
TRAP: choosing A because it has more words. Fix: ask which one you can picture, student votes again.
CLARIFY: if a student says harm is a verb too, say yes, but do harm could mean a scratch or worse - choke shows exactly what.
---
Purpose: guided judgement between a vague and an exact verb. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: the test is always the same question - can the reader see exactly what happens?

you_do.title: Upgrade the vague verb
you_do.rule: Write the exact verb in your OG book.

round.prompt:
Rubbish gets into the drains
after every storm.
round.why: it shows exactly how the rubbish moves
round.notes:

1. SAY: "Read it in your head, then write just the verb in your OG book. Pens down when you are done."
2. TIME: 30 sec. SCAN four books near you. 80%+ -> click to reveal. Less -> ask which verb can sit in front of into the drains and show how it moves, then re-ask.
3. REVEAL after books are scanned. SAY: "Tick it or fix it. Gets is vague and goes is still vague. Washes shows exactly how the rubbish moves."
TRAP: choosing goes. Fix: ask, does goes show HOW it moves? Student swaps to washes.
EXTENSION: Write the whole sentence with your verb, then write a second sentence about the drains with another exact verb of your own.
HELP: cover one wrong chip so the student chooses between two, then reads the sentence aloud with each.

3. REVEAL after books are scanned. SAY: "Tick it or fix it. Going away is vague. Melting shows exactly what happens to the ice when it warms."

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Swap vague verbs like gets, goes, makes and says for verbs that show exactly what happens, with a strength that fits the facts.
WHY THIS WEEK: last week's nouns told the reader exactly who or what. Vague verbs still make an argument sound flat, because the reader cannot see what is happening.
TIME: 5 minutes, no more - I do 1 min, We do 1 question, You do 3 questions at about 45 seconds each. One question per slide; your click reveals the answer.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards - books, fingers and voices only.
PREP: a verb is the doing or saying word. Three upgrades this week: exact (exactly what happens?), strength (does it fit the facts? too strong is hyperbole), saying verbs (how was it said?).

i_do.title: Pick the right strength
i_do.rule: Choose a verb strong enough to persuade, but true to the facts.
i_do.example:
Fact: lunch is now 10 minutes shorter.
The rule destroys our lunch. (too strong)
The rule cuts our lunch. (fits the facts)
items: Too weak: changes. Too strong: destroys.
Ask: does it fit the facts?
i_do.footer: Tomorrow: verbs that show how it was said
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: cuts fits - destroys is too strong for ten minutes, which makes it hyperbole.
1. SAY: "Okay, yesterday we made verbs exact. Today, strength. Too weak and nobody cares; too strong and your reader stops believing you."
2. WRITE: copy the fact and "The rule destroys our lunch." on the class board. POINT at destroys and ask aloud, did lunch disappear?
3. WRITE: cross out destroys and write cuts above it, so the board reads "The rule cuts our lunch." Tick it beside the fact.
4. ASK: "Hyper means over. Is destroys over the top here? Thumbs up or down, voices off, on three." 5 sec. EXPECT: thumbs up - it is hyperbole.
TRAP: thinking the strongest verb always wins. Fix: point at the fact, ask what really happened, student picks the verb that matches.
CLARIFY: if a student asks when destroys would be right, say only if lunch was cancelled completely - then the facts would back it up.
---

terrain - terr means land + -ain makes it a thing: the land itself and its shape. Hills, rocks and mud are the terrain you run across.

terrier - terr means land + -ier means one that: one that goes into the land. A small dog bred to dig into burrows after rabbits.
subterranean - sub means under + terr means land + -anean means relating to: relating to under the land. Underground, like a wombat burrow.
terraform - terr means land + form means shape: to shape land - to change another planet until it is like Earth. Science fiction, for now.

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
READ each word as it appears, then connect terr to the card meaning: land.
territorial - terr means land + -ory means a place for + -ial means relating to: relating to a place of land you guard. Magpies get territorial in spring.
territories - terr means land + -ory means a place for + -ies means more than one: places of land. Australia has two mainland territories, the NT and the ACT.
terraced - terr means land + -ace + -ed: land cut into flat steps. A terraced garden climbs the hill step by step.
terrariums - terr means land + -arium means a place for + -s: places for land, more than one. Our science room could hold two terrariums.
terriers - terr means land + -ier means one that + -s: dogs that go into the land. Terriers dig.
terrestrial - terr means land + -estr means belonging to + -ial means relating to: relating to things that belong on land. Emus are terrestrial birds - they cannot fly.
subterranean - sub means under + terr means land + -anean means relating to: relating to under the land. Subterranean water sits in rock under our feet.
terracotta - terr means land + cotta means cooked: cooked land. A terracotta pot is baked earth.
terraform - terr means land + form means shape: to shape land, changing a planet until it is like Earth.
Memory hook: stamp your foot when you say terr - the land under your feet. Can't stamp on it? It is a look-alike, like terrible. Challenge: bring one more terr word by Thursday.

EXTENSION: Then move the subordinate clause to the end of the sentence and fix the punctuation.
Answer: e.g. Because magpies are territorial, the terraced garden is closed in spring. / The terraced garden is closed in spring because magpies are territorial.

words_to_spell_review.prompt: astro means star. Why would a huge price be called astronomical?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Because it is as huge as the distances between the stars.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Mr Lee put an asterisk beside the trickiest question on the quiz.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: aster means star. Which part of asterisk makes the star little?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -isk ending, meaning little. An asterisk is a little star, like this *.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: We ate lunch on the stone terrace above the school garden.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: terr means land. What shape of land is a terrace?
words_to_spell_review.answer: A flat step of land, like one stair cut into the side of a hill.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Kangaroos are terrestrial animals, but dolphins spend their whole lives in the sea.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: terr means land. So where does a terrestrial animal live?
words_to_spell_review.answer: On the land. The -ial ending means relating to, so terrestrial means relating to the land.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our class website has every homework sheet hyperlinked on one page.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which part tells you each link jumps you over to another page?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The hyper part, meaning over. The -ed ending tells you the linking is already done.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The omnipresence of seagulls at the beach made eating chips a real challenge.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: omni means all. Which taught ending turns present into a thing you can name?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -ence ending, the same one in dependence. Omnipresence means being present everywhere.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Forgetting your hat is not an excuse to miss out on sport.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: cus means cause. What is an excuse trying to give?
words_to_spell_review.answer: A cause, or a reason, that gets you out of something. The ex part means out.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: In the courtroom drama, the accuser pointed straight at the butler.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: cus means cause. What is the accuser saying about the butler?
words_to_spell_review.answer: That the butler caused the crime. The -er ending names the person doing the accusing.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The battery is the most important component of our science buggy.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pon means place. Where is a component placed?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Inside something bigger. It is one part of the whole machine, like the battery in the buggy.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Choosing teams only from your friends can be a kind of prejudice.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pre means before and jud means judge. When does prejudice make its judgement?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Before knowing the facts. The judging comes first, so the facts never get a turn.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Week review - ask the three verb questions of one argument sentence, then upgrade it.
WHY THIS WEEK: vague verbs make an argument flat and too-strong verbs make readers stop trusting it; the three questions fix both.
TIME: 5 minutes, no more - I do 1 min, We do 1 question, You do 3 questions at about 45 seconds each. One question per slide; your click reveals the answer.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards - books, fingers and voices only.
PREP: exact (exactly what happens?), strength (does it fit the facts? too strong is hyperbole), saying verbs (how was it said?).

i_do.title: Upgrade every verb
i_do.rule: Ask three questions: exactly what? Fits the facts? How was it said?
i_do.example:
Fact: two pies were burnt.
The chef says the oven ruined every pie.
The chef admits the oven burnt two pies.
items: Exact: washes, digs. Strength: fits the facts.
Saying: warn, insist, agree, admit, show.
i_do.footer: Next week: upgrade your own argument
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: says becomes admits (how it was said) and ruined every becomes burnt two (fits the facts).
1. SAY: "Okay, this week we upgraded verbs three ways. Today one sentence needs two of them, so ask all three questions."
2. WRITE: copy the fact and "The chef says the oven ruined every pie." on the class board. POINT at ruined every and ask, does it fit the facts?
3. WRITE: cross out ruined every and write burnt two, then cross out says and write admits, so the board matches the bottom line.
4. ASK: "Why admits, not says? Turn and tell your partner." 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: the chef did not want to say it - it is the chef's own oven.
TRAP: fixing only the first verb you see. Fix: say ask all three questions of every verb, student rereads and finds the second.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether ruined is ever right, say yes, if every pie really was burnt - the fact decides.
---
Purpose: week review restates all three upgrades on one argument sentence (absent-student rule). [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: exact (washes for gets), strength (burnt two, not ruined every), saying verb (admits for says).

we_do.title: Which verb fits the facts?
we_do.rule: Pick the sentence whose verb fits the facts.

round.prompt:
Fact: the library closed for one day.
A) The flood destroyed our library.
B) The flood closed our library.
round.why: closed for one day, not destroyed
round.notes:
ANSWER: B - closed fits the fact.
1. SAY: "Okay, read the fact first, then both sentences, in your head."
2. ASK: "Which verb fits the facts? One finger for A, two for B, voices off, show me on three." 5 sec. EXPECT: two fingers - B.
3. REVEAL after fingers are scanned. ASK: "Which of the three questions did you use?" Cold call one student. EXPECT: does it fit the facts - the strength question.
4. WRITE: copy A on the class board, cross out destroyed and write closed, so it matches the fact.
TRAP: choosing A because a flood sounds serious. Fix: point at one day, ask whether the library is gone, student votes again.
CLARIFY: if a student says closed sounds boring, say it is exactly as strong as the facts, so the reader trusts you.
---
Purpose: guided strength check, the question most often skipped. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: the fact decides; a verb stronger than the facts is hyperbole.

you_do.title: Upgrade the verb
you_do.rule: Write the best verb in your OG book. Ask the three questions.

round.prompt:
Strong wind does damage to
our vegetable garden.
round.why: it shows exactly what the wind does
round.notes:
ANSWER: flattens.
1. SAY: "Read it in your head, then write just the verb in your OG book. Pens down when you are done."
2. TIME: 30 sec. SCAN four books near you. 80%+ -> click to reveal. Less -> ask exactly what strong wind does to tall plants, then re-ask.
3. REVEAL after books are scanned. SAY: "Tick it or fix it. Does damage to is vague. Flattens shows exactly what the wind does to the plants - the exact question."
TRAP: choosing makes. Fix: ask, makes what? Student swaps to flattens.
EXTENSION: Write the whole sentence, then name which of the three questions fixed it.
HELP: give the student the three questions on a card and ask them to try each one aloud on the verb.
---
Purpose: exact-verb question first, easy case. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]

round.prompt:
The rain gauge ____ that we had
40 mm of rain this week.
round.why: a gauge measures, so it shows
round.notes:
ANSWER: shows.
1. SAY: "Read it in your head, then write just the verb in your OG book. Pens down when you are done."
2. TIME: 30 sec. SCAN four books near you. 80%+ -> click to reveal. Less -> ask whether a gauge talks or measures, then re-ask.
3. REVEAL after books are scanned. SAY: "Tick it or fix it. A gauge cannot talk - it measures. Evidence shows, so the gauge shows we had 40 mm of rain."
TRAP: choosing says. Fix: ask, can a gauge say anything? Student swaps to shows.
---
Purpose: saying-verb question for evidence, not a person. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]

round.prompt:
Fact: the bus was five minutes late.
The bus ____ our excursion.
round.why: five minutes late is delayed, not wrecked
round.notes:
ANSWER: delayed.
1. SAY: "Read it in your head, then write just the verb in your OG book. Pens down when you are done."
2. TIME: 30 sec. SCAN four books near you. 80%+ -> click to reveal. Less -> ask whether five minutes late wrecks a whole excursion, then re-ask.
3. REVEAL after books are scanned. SAY: "Tick it or fix it. Changed is too weak and wrecked is hyperbole for five minutes. Delayed fits the fact - the strength question."
4. SAY: "Before you hand in your argument, ask the three questions of every verb. Upgrade one verb on every line."
TRAP: choosing wrecked. Fix: point at five minutes, ask whether the excursion was wrecked, student swaps to delayed.
EXTENSION: Take three verbs from your persuasive writing, upgrade each one, and label which question each upgrade answers.
---
Purpose: edge case: strength against a fact, and the verb stays in the past. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
